keyVerseText: Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee. that: Heb. from having compassion
rootMeaning: The root of עוּל (ʻûwl) is connected to the act of suckling or nursing, derived from the verb עוּל which means to give suck or nurse. This etymology highlights the intimate, nurturing relationship between a mother and her infant, emphasizing not just infancy but the dependency and care involved in early life. The literal root sense conveys more than just a young child; it evokes the tender, life-sustaining act of feeding and protection.
usageInScripture: The word עוּל appears only twice in Scripture, consistently referring to a very young child, specifically an infant who is still nursing. Translations such as 'her sucking child' and 'There shall be no more thence an infant' show a focus on the vulnerability and dependence of a suckling child. This limited but consistent usage underscores the concept of infancy as a stage marked by need and care, rather than mere chronological age.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding עוּל as a suckling child enriches our grasp of biblical imagery concerning God's care and compassion. The term evokes the helplessness of infancy, reminding believers of their own dependence on divine provision and nurture. It also highlights the tender, covenantal love God has for His people, akin to a mother’s care for her nursing child. This word points to the faithfulness of God who, unlike human frailty, never forgets or abandons those who are vulnerable and dependent on Him.
keyVerseReflection: Isaiah 49:15 asks, 'Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb?' The use of עוּל here emphasizes the deep, instinctual bond between mother and infant, underscoring the depth of God's compassion. The verse reassures that even if a mother could forget her nursing child, God’s remembrance and compassion toward His people are unfailing. The word strengthens the metaphor of divine faithfulness and tender care.
